summary: Defines the encapsulation for MPLS performance measurement with the Alternate-Marking Method, which does flow-based packet loss, delay and jitter measurement on MPLS traffic.

eli5.summary: Packets get painted one color for a while and then another, so you can count them and time them by color to see what is lost or slow.

subtitle: A three-word MPLS label stack entry that tags packets with a flow ID and a color so routers can count loss and time delay.

tldr.problem: The Alternate-Marking Method can measure packet loss, delay and jitter by coloring batches of packets, but MPLS had no defined way to carry the flow identifier and color bits.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC places an Extension Label, a new Flow-ID Label Indicator (value 18) and a Flow-ID Label in the label stack. The Flow-ID Label carries a flow ID plus L, D and T bits in the traffic class bit positions.
tldr.outcome: Edge or transit routers can find the flow, read the color and export counters and timestamps. The MPLS Working Group has agreed to make this document Historic once the MPLS Network Actions solution is published.

today: RFC 9714 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2025, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text says the MPLS Working Group has agreed to make it Historic when the MNA solution is published as an RFC.

sections.title: Why MPLS Needs an Encapsulation
sections.content:
RFC 9341 describes the Alternate-Marking Method, which measures packet loss, delay and jitter by marking consecutive batches of packets. RFC 8372 outlines considerations for identifying MPLS flows for performance monitoring.

This document defines the MPLS encapsulation for the method. It supports monitoring at intermediate nodes and flow identification at both the transport and service layers.

The RFC notes that work on MPLS Network Actions (MNAs, RFC 9613) was ongoing. MNA is expected to provide a more advanced solution with broader applicability, and the MPLS Working Group agreed that this document will be made Historic when that solution is published as an RFC.
sections.eli5: Counting colored packages is a good idea, but MPLS needed a place on the package to hold the name tag and sticker. This RFC picks that place.

sections.title: The Flow-ID Label Encapsulation
sections.content:
The encapsulation is three consecutive label stack entries. First comes the Extension Label (XL, value 15). Next is the Flow-ID Label Indicator (FLI), an Extended Special Purpose Label that the RFC defines as value 18; together with the XL it forms a Composite Special Purpose Label (cSPL, RFC 9017). Last is the Flow-ID Label (FL), which identifies the flow.

The TC and TTL of the XL and FLI MUST copy the label immediately preceding the XL, and their BoS bit MUST be zero. A node that processes an XL or FLI with BoS set MUST discard the packet and MAY log an error.

The FL value MUST be unique within the administrative domain, with a one-to-one mapping between Flow-ID and flow. Its TTL MUST be zero so it is never used for forwarding. Its BoS bit is set only when it is at the bottom of the stack. The FL can sit at the bottom or in the middle of the stack but not at the top, and it MAY appear several times.

The three traffic class bits of the FL are repurposed: L colors packets for loss measurement (set is color 1, unset is color 0), D colors packets for delay and jitter measurement, and T says whether the measurement is edge-to-edge (1) or hop-by-hop (0).
sections.eli5: Three small tags are stuck on the packet: one says a special tag follows, one says which kind, and the last holds the flow's name and its color stickers.

sections.title: Where the Flow-ID Label Goes in the Stack
sections.content:
The RFC shows three example layouts, each using a 4-octet FL, and notes that more may exist. For transport, the cSPL and FL sit below the LSP label and above the application label. For service, they sit below the application label, which can be a pseudowire, Ethernet VPN or IP VPN label. For both, two sets appear, and the two FL values must be different and are independent of each other.

Penultimate hop popping (PHP) needs care. A node must pop the XL, FLI and FL when it pops the preceding forwarding label, so the penultimate router would remove them and the egress router would be excluded from measurement. PHP should be disabled unless the penultimate router is known to support this and excluding the egress is acceptable.
sections.eli5: The tags can go in different spots in a stack of tags, depending on whether you track the road trip, the delivery job, or both.

sections.title: Encapsulation, Look-Up and Decapsulation
sections.content:
The ingress node inserts the XL, FLI and FL and sets the FL value, the color bits and the T bit.

With edge-to-edge measurement (T is 1), only the ingress and egress nodes process the label. Otherwise every MPLS node along the LSP is a processing node. A processing node finds the FL using the XL and FLI, and exports data such as the Flow-ID, block counters and timestamps to an external NMS or controller. The export method is outside the scope. A transit node must look beyond the top forwarding label to do this.

A processing node MUST pop the XL, FLI and FL when it pops the preceding forwarding label. The egress node MUST pop the whole stack.
sections.eli5: The first stop sticks on the tags. Stops that are told to watch for them write down what they see and report it to a manager.

sections.title: Allocating Flow-IDs
sections.content:
The RFC describes at least two ways to allocate a Flow-ID. With a manual trigger, an operator enters the flow's characteristics (such as the IP five tuple and DSCP) and the NMS or controller generates one or two Flow-IDs and provisions the ingress node. With an automatic trigger, the ingress node spots the flow and reports its characteristics to the controller using IPFIX (RFC 7011), and the controller allocates and provisions the Flow-ID.

Policy decides whether one or two Flow-IDs are generated: one for the MPLS service, one for the transport, or both. When both exist, a transit node looks up both by default, though configuration can change that.

Every Flow-ID MUST be unique within the administrative domain and MUST NOT be in the reserved label space (0-15).
sections.eli5: A manager hands out unique name tags, either when a person asks or when the first stop notices a new package.

sections.title: Label Depth and Multipath Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC defines the Flow-ID Label Capability (FLC) and Flow-ID Readable Label Depth (FRLD), analogous to the entropy label capability and readable depth (RFC 6790, RFC 8662). The ingress node MUST insert each FL deep enough that the node exposing it has the FLC, and SHOULD insert it within the minimum FRLD of the on-path nodes that need to read it. With Segment Routing, long stacks can make this hard, so an implementation MAY place identical FLs between SID labels.

Under equal-cost multipath, adding an FL to an existing flow may move it to a different path, the same problem as with the Synonymous Flow Label (RFC 8957). Operators can apply entropy labels or add the FL to all flows.
sections.eli5: Not every stop can read tags buried deep in the stack, so the first stop must place them where later stops can see them.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
Following RFC 9341, the method and this encapsulation MUST only be applied to controlled domains, or the attacks discussed in Section 10 of RFC 9341 may apply. An FL's scope is its administrative domain, and it MUST NOT be signaled or distributed outside it, because leaking would cause Flow-ID conflicts.

Domain boundary nodes MUST use policies such as ACLs: at the sending edge they MUST filter out packets carrying the FLI that go to other domains, and at the receiving edge they MUST drop packets carrying the FLI from other domains. The RFC states that leakage is neither a privacy breach nor a source of DoS.

IANA assigned value 18, Flow-ID Label Indicator (FLI), in the Extended Special-Purpose MPLS Label Values registry.
sections.eli5: The tags are only meant for your own network, so the doors in and out of it must block packets wearing them.
